entities.name: George Orwell
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
George Orwell (1903–1950), born Eric Arthur Blair, was an English novelist, essayist, and critic whose works 'Animal Farm' (1945) and 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' (1949) are the two most influential political novels of the 20th century. His name became an adjective—'Orwellian'—denoting the surveillance state, propaganda, and linguistic manipulation he warned against.

Orwell served as an Imperial Police officer in Burma, fought with the POUM militia in the Spanish Civil War (where he was shot through the throat), and lived deliberately among the poor in Paris and London. These experiences forged his commitment to democratic socialism and his hatred of totalitarianism in all forms.

'Animal Farm' (1945) satirised the Soviet revolution as a farmyard fable. 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' (1949)—written while dying of tuberculosis on the Scottish island of Jura—gave the world Big Brother, doublethink, thoughtcrime, and Newspeak. The novel has sold over 50 million copies and surges in sales whenever authoritarianism rises.

Orwell's six rules for clear writing ('Politics and the English Language,' 1946) remain the gold standard for prose style. As Christopher Hitchens wrote: 'He faced the totalitarian threat with an understanding that was superior to that of the professionals.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Orwell's works warned against totalitarianism and propaganda, shaping the Cold War narrative and influencing democratic movements worldwide. His writing has been translated into over 60 languages, with 'Nineteen Eighty-Four' being a top-10 bestseller in the UK since its publication.
